why.explorer: Lemons are sour. Sour helps the zap move!
why.builder: Lemon juice is full of acid. Acid is packed with tiny charged bits that can carry electricity from one nail to the other.
why.engineer: Citric acid dissociates into mobile ions, so the flesh conducts. Zinc gives up electrons more readily than copper, and that difference is the cell voltage.

guessPrompt.explorer: Will the lemon make the light glow?
guessPrompt.builder: Sour things usually conduct well. Guess: strong, medium, or weak?
guessPrompt.engineer: Predict the open-circuit voltage before you measure. Then predict what happens to current.

why.explorer: Potatoes work too, but not as well.
why.builder: A potato is not sour, but it still has juice with charged bits in it. It just fights back harder than a lemon.
why.engineer: Phosphoric acid electrolyte with a starchy matrix - higher internal resistance than citrus. Boiling the potato first ruptures cell walls and measurably improves output.

guessPrompt.explorer: Potato or lemon - which is stronger?
guessPrompt.builder: Do you think a potato beats a lemon? Guess first, then test.
guessPrompt.engineer: Predict whether the potato's higher internal resistance shows up more in voltage or in current.

why.explorer: Apples are only a little bit sour.
why.builder: An apple is sweet, not sour, so it has fewer charged bits than a lemon. It's a weaker battery but still conducts.
why.engineer: Malic acid at lower concentration than citrus. Good middle-of-the-table result for the leaderboard.

guessPrompt.explorer: Do you think the apple will work?
guessPrompt.builder: Sweet instead of sour. Better or worse than the lemon?
guessPrompt.engineer: Rank apple against lemon and potato before measuring.

why.explorer: Pickles are super salty. Salt loves electricity!
why.builder: A pickle has been sitting in salty water for weeks, so it is stuffed with salt. Salt is brilliant at carrying electricity - this is usually the leaderboard winner.
why.engineer: Brine-saturated, so it has by far the highest free-ion concentration on the table. Expect it to be an order of magnitude less resistive than fresh fruit.

guessPrompt.builder: This one has a secret weapon. Can you guess what it is?
guessPrompt.engineer: Predict the pickle's resistance relative to the lemon. Justify it from ion concentration.

why.explorer: Salty water is a super highway for the zap.
why.builder: Plain water is bad at carrying electricity. Stir salt into it and it becomes great at it. The salt is doing all the work, not the water.
why.engineer: NaCl dissociates into Na+ and Cl- ions. Conductivity scales with concentration - this is the control that proves it is the ions conducting, not the water.

guessPrompt.explorer: Salty water or plain water - which is better?
guessPrompt.builder: Test plain water first, then stir in salt and test again. What changed?
guessPrompt.engineer: Measure at three salt concentrations and see whether resistance falls linearly.

why.explorer: Plain water is not very good at all!
why.builder: Surprise! Pure water is actually a bad carrier of electricity. It only works when something is dissolved in it.
why.engineer: Deionised water is near-insulating. Tap water conducts only through dissolved mineral ions, so readings vary a lot by region.

guessPrompt.explorer: Is water good at electricity? Guess!
guessPrompt.builder: Most people guess wrong on this one. Write your guess down first.
guessPrompt.engineer: Predict tap water vs salt water, then explain the gap.

why.explorer: Squishy banana. Not a very good one!
why.builder: Bananas are mostly starch and sugar, not acid, so not much electricity gets through.
why.engineer: Low free-ion content relative to citrus. Interesting variable: a very ripe banana measures differently from a green one.

guessPrompt.builder: Try a ripe one and a green one. Do they score the same?
guessPrompt.engineer: Test ripeness as a variable and record both.

why.explorer: Crunchy celery is full of water.
why.builder: Celery is mostly water with minerals in it, so it's an okay middle-of-the-pack conductor.
why.engineer: High water content with dissolved salts. Try probing along the stalk versus across it - the fibres make it directional.

guessPrompt.builder: Try poking along the stringy bits, then across them. Any difference?
guessPrompt.engineer: Test for anisotropy: measure along the vascular bundles and across them.

why.explorer: You are a little bit zappy too!
why.builder: You are mostly salty water, so you conduct - but your dry skin is a good blocker. Lick your finger and you conduct much better.
why.engineer: Dry skin is the dominant resistance, typically megohms. Moisture drops it sharply, which is exactly why the transistor touch switch responds to a damp finger.

guessPrompt.explorer: Are YOU part of the circuit?
guessPrompt.builder: Measure with a dry finger, then a damp one. Big difference?
guessPrompt.engineer: Compare dry vs damp skin and explain which layer dominates the measurement.
